/world/2026/oct/18/french-government-cri.headline: Buildings set ablaze and more than 1,800 arrested as police clash with protesters across France
/world/2026/oct/18/french-government-cri.excerpt: More than 1,800 people were arrested in France on Saturday after protesters supporting high school students clashed with police, with some demonstrations later spiralling out of control as buildings were set ablaze and shops looted. Police fired teargas in confrontations with protesters, as demonstrations across France were boosted by other groups angry about high prices and the fraying of a social welfare system. While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully in street marches in scores of cities, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers. Late on Saturday, prime minister Sébastien Lecornu said 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police hurt. On Sunday interior minister Laurent Nuñez announced that the number of arrests had gone up to 1,800. Nuñez said the official demonstration had been hijacked by casseurs – “opportunistic delinquents who had seen a chance to pillage and loot … we will find them and deal with them firmly”. He said the state was not planning to declare a state of emergency but added: “I very strongly condemn the violence we have seen.” In the city of Limoges, the town hall was “largely lost” to a fire set by masked protesters, the top regional official told the AFP news agency.
/world/2026/oct/18/french-government-cri.trail: Police fire teargas in Paris and Limoges town hall ‘largely lost’ to fire – with officials blaming violence on ‘ultra-left’

/world/2026/oct/18/french-government-cri.headline: Fire destroys Marché des Enfants Rouges, ‘coolest market in Paris’
/world/2026/oct/18/french-government-cri.excerpt: Fire has ravaged Paris’s oldest surviving covered food market, a popular street food venue dating back to the 17th century in the Marais district of the French capital that drew thousands of locals and tourists daily. Ariel Weil, the central Paris mayor, said the Marché des Enfants ‌Rouges had been “totally destroyed” in the blaze, which broke out soon after 3am. “The worst was avoided: the fire did not spread to the surrounding buildings,” he said. “But there is a lot of emotion. A lot of sadness.” The market was established in 1615 during the reign of Louis XIII and took its name from a nearby orphanage, the Hospice des Enfants Rouges – founded in 1536 by King Francis I and his sister Marguerite de Navarre – whose child residents were habitually dressed in red. The structure was listed as a historic monument in 1982 but narrowly escaped demolition shortly afterwards when Paris city hall, led by the then mayor, Jacques Chirac, approved radical redevelopment plans that would have replaced it with an underground car park, a council daycare facility and community centre. A determined campaign by local residents and neighbourhood associations, backed by intellectuals, writers and artists including film-makers and photographers such as Bertrand Tavernier and Willy Ronis, who captured its traders on camera, gathered tens of thousands of signatures in protest and the plans were eventually abandoned in the mid-1990s.
/world/2026/oct/18/french-government-cri.trail: ‘A lot of sadness’ after 17th century landmark that escaped demolition in the 1980s goes up in flames

/world/2026/oct/18/french-government-cri.headline: Remember Me review – narrow view of two photographic centuries is like a history of food in three ham sarnies
/world/2026/oct/18/french-government-cri.excerpt: ‘Beware … of assuming the sterile attitude of the spectator, for life is not a spectacle” scream the words of Aimé Césaire – writ large and bold by Barbara Kruger, in a giant installation, The History of Tears, that fills Bourse de Commerce’s spectacular Rotunda. Kruger’s angry, menacing, viscerally charged work – words as images, and large-scale video clips of people seething with self-hate – is a thrilling setup for Remember Me, an exhibition that promises a take on 200 years of photography through 700 works by more than 70 artists drawn from the collection of the French billionaire François Pinault. That excitement quickly dissipates as the exhibition moves on. This is the biggest photography show ever held at the Bourse de Commerce. Remember Me has two main problems: first, it tries to say too much with too few artists. For a start, nearly 450 of the 700 or so works are by Irving Penn. It leans heavily on classical, conventional approaches, styles and familiar names, and that creates a very obvious skew in the perception of what photography is, does, and how it is presented. The organisation makes no real sense. There are two main spaces, in addition to Kruger’s installation, dedicated exclusively to one artist. Penn is one of them. The installation looks undeniably beautiful: following the curving Ando architecture, the works have been hung like waves, expanding in undulating lines across the walls, without chronology or theme, flowing freely into the space.
/world/2026/oct/18/french-government-cri.trail: There are 700 works from François Pinault’s collection on display – more than half of them by Irving Penn – but it’s a blinkered selection and annoyingly didactic

/world/2026/oct/18/french-government-cri.headline: Thursday briefing: Why young people are taking to the streets across France
/world/2026/oct/18/french-government-cri.excerpt: Good morning. In my experience, at any protest, the most memorable and encapsulating slogans are always the ones written by hand with marker pen on cardboard placards. “School is a right, not a privilege,” read one such sign held aloft by a student in Paris, where huge youth protests over the state of high school education have brought tens of thousands of young people and adults on to the streets, with further strikes planned today. “A state that gasses high school students is a weak state,” another sign said, referencing growing public anger at alleged police brutality towards young protesters. Tens of thousands of young people have also taken to Spanish streets in recent weeks to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis. And outside the Labour conference in Liverpool last week, a crowd of jobless young people protested against what they saw as their bleak employment prospects. From Paris to the north of England, a similar thread runs through it all: a generation who feel betrayed by the absence of basic economic security and the erosion of public services that older generations took for granted. I spoke to our Paris correspondent Angelique Chrisafis who has been reporting from the centre of the French protests. But first, the headlines. Five big stories UK politics | Kemi Badenoch has announced that the Conservatives would abolish inheritance tax on family homes if elected, prompting criticism that she is prioritising cutting taxes for the rich.
/world/2026/oct/18/french-government-cri.trail: In today’s newsletter: A youth-led movement is protesting crumbling school buildings and teacher shortages while turning adult focus onto wider educational inequalities

/world/2026/oct/18/french-government-cri.headline: Riot police fire teargas as 250,000 take part in schools protests across France
/world/2026/oct/18/french-government-cri.excerpt: Police have fired teargas at ⁠protesters as more than 250,000 pupils, teachers and parents demonstrated across France on the biggest day yet of a campaign for better high school conditions that has been marred by often violent clashes with police. The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said at least 215 teenagers and 85 school staff had been injured since the protests began more than a fortnight ago, calling the figures “the heaviest ⁠toll in decades paid by the school system”. The country’s president, Emmanuel Macron, called key ministers to the Élysée Palace for talks on Tuesday night, French media reported. The interior ministry said 200,000 people had taken part in mainly peaceful marches in cities including Marseille, Nantes ⁠and Lyon on Tuesday, with 56,000 more joining the biggest demonstration in Paris. Organisers put the total at 450,000. Most passed off without serious incident, but some – including in Paris – ended in sporadic vandalism and running skirmishes with riot police, with officers firing teargas and carrying out baton charges to disperse protesters. Nearly 500 people were arrested on Tuesday, according to figures from the Interior Ministry reported by newspaper Liberation. The ministry also said 43 police officers were injured.
/world/2026/oct/18/french-government-cri.trail: Officers also carry out baton charges as students, staff and parents march in cities including Paris, Marseille and Lyon

/society/2026/oct/18/cut-benefits-fund-e.headline: Key disability benefit for young people may be axed under major welfare changes
/society/2026/oct/18/cut-benefits-fund-e.excerpt: Ministers are working up sweeping plans for welfare changes including scrapping a key disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work, the Guardian has learned. Whitehall sources said the package of changes under debate was much bigger than previously thought, as Andy Burnham’s government hopes to persuade more people on benefits back into work. The move could be fraught with political danger after last year’s dramatic welfare rebellion by Labour MPs. But ministers have spent weeks trying to persuade them the plans are about reform, and feel confident opposition has waned. The plans are still awaiting the conclusions of reviews by Alan Milburn, who is looking at young people’s employment, and the Timms panel, which is examining the personal independence payment (Pip), a non-means-tested benefit that helps sick and disabled people with support costs. However, a central option under consideration for young people is removing the health element of universal credit for claimants under 25, which has already been almost halved to £217 a month, and offering intensive support for people to get into work. The possibility of removing it for existing claimants – not just new ones – is being looked at.
/society/2026/oct/18/cut-benefits-fund-e.trail: Exclusive: Plan under discussion involves intensive support to help young people into employment

/society/2026/oct/18/cut-benefits-fund-e.headline: ‘Work is good for you’: how UK scheme could help tackle youth mental health crisis
/society/2026/oct/18/cut-benefits-fund-e.excerpt: Work must be “part of the answer” to the mental health crisis among young people, the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, has said as he met some of the first beneficiaries of Labour’s youth jobs guarantee scheme. He was speaking on a visit to Boots’s headquarters in Nottingham on Wednesday, where several 18- to 21-year-olds were taken on under the job guarantee – with their wages paid by the taxpayer for six months. Some of the recruits were packing and labelling boxes of products to be posted out to households, and others are in administrative roles. They told McFadden about long periods of fruitless jobhunting. “It was just amazing for me to hear their stories,” McFadden said of the recruits. “These are young people who have been out of work for one, two, up to four years. Most of them have been working here for a few weeks. And you can already see how it’s changed their confidence in themselves – their sense of belief in themselves.” A rise in cases of mental illness is widely cited as one cause for the increase in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) in recent years. But McFadden said the reasons could run the other way, too. “Work is part of the answer. Work is good for you. It’s bad for your mental health to be sitting at home, isolated. “I see this not only as an economic thing, but as a response to greater instances of mental health problems for young people.
/society/2026/oct/18/cut-benefits-fund-e.trail: Paid employment can boost confidence and wellbeing, says Pat McFadden as jobs guarantee scheme gets under way

/world/2026/oct/19/britain-geopolitical-.headline: ‘I felt disgusted’: MEP speaks out over nude deepfakes and urges EU action
/world/2026/oct/19/britain-geopolitical-.excerpt: An Austrian MEP has spoken out about her experience of being “stripped naked” online without her consent and has urged the EU to take action, as a report found that one in six female MEPs had been targeted by sexualised AI-generated content. Lena Schilling of the Green party said she had learned last month about nude deepfakes of herself circulating online. When she opened the links, she found herself staring at images from one of her first ever press conferences – but the images had been digitally altered to remove her clothing. It was a shocking twist on a defining moment of her career. “I felt disgusted,” she said. “I remember how nervous I was and how much I had prepared for the press conference. And then to see someone using this image in a way aimed at harming and humiliating me was really hard to grasp.” Schilling is one of 50 MEPs – 46 of them women – who have been targeted by sexualised deepfakes, according to a report by Agora Digitale Transformation (ADT). The Berlin-based thinktank, which alerted Schilling to the presence of the images online, said the finding laid bare how deepfake pornography had become a “systemic threat to women in European politics”. An earlier ADT report found that 138 female parliamentarians from 22 EU countries had been affected, and that women were 33 times more likely than their male colleagues to be depicted in or associated with deepfake pornography.
/world/2026/oct/19/britain-geopolitical-.trail: Lena Schilling of Austrian Greens says images are ‘digital violence against women’ and a threat to democracy

/world/2026/oct/19/britain-geopolitical-.headline: Briton threatened with deportation from Sweden over Brexit rules goes into hiding
/world/2026/oct/19/britain-geopolitical-.excerpt: A seriously ill British man living in Sweden has been forced into hiding amid fears he will be deported as a result of what he says is a government Brexit residency error. Mark Smith, 60, who has had heart attacks, strokes, severe headaches and chronically high blood pressure that has been difficult to treat, was told on the phone he should leave Sweden by 17 October as he was an “alien” without permission to stay. Terrified of deportation, he and his wife have moved out of their home in Falkenberg, in south-west Sweden, to a caravan park. “We are in hiding, we daren’t go back to our apartment. We are scared to go out as we don’t know if the police will come and take us,” Smith said. A court ruled on 12 October that a decision on deportation would not be suspended but gave him until 20 October to “submit his application for a retrial” in relation to “the grounds for the decision on indefinite deportation”. Smith has been in Sweden since 2017 and says he was told by authorities he did not need to do anything to stay after Brexit in 2020. He worked, had private health insurance, supported his wife and registered on the population register administered by the national tax authority, as required under Swedish rules. He was unaware, however, that Sweden was among 13 of the 27 EU member states that required Britons living in the country before Brexit to make a formal application to remain.
/world/2026/oct/19/britain-geopolitical-.trail: Mark Smith, who has severe health issues, says he was told three times he needed to do nothing in order to remain after Brexit

/world/2026/oct/19/britain-geopolitical-.headline: Brexit’s back – but are British voters ready to contemplate a reversal?
/world/2026/oct/19/britain-geopolitical-.excerpt: In February 2016, days after David Cameron announced the UK would hold a referendum on leaving the EU, he told workers in Slough not to imagine they could change their minds a few years down the line if they did not like how things panned out. Voting to stay in or leave was a once in a generation thing, he said. “This is a decision that lasts for life.” Well times change, as the last prime minister but five could testify. A decade after Britain told Brussels where to go, Brexit is back on the political agenda. After years in which many politicians avoided any mention of the B-word, Andy Burnham broke the omertà in his party conference speech last month, saying he would look again at Britain’s relationship with Europe. This week he went further, insisting the current arrangement must change: “Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain.” Among a range of options on the table, he has been clear, is the possibility of going “all the way” and rejoining the EU. There are pressing economic reasons Burnham has been talking up closer alignment, as the EU works out its position on the UK’s access to its protectionist “Made in Europe” legislation, which the prime minister has said could hurt British manufacturing. But after years of bitter division and political dysfunction in the fallout from the vote, are the British public really ready to talk about Brexit again – and even to contemplate reversing it? Polling evidence may suggest so.
/world/2026/oct/19/britain-geopolitical-.trail: As Andy Burnham talks up closer alignment with the EU and a poll suggests half in UK would rejoin, the B-word is back on the agenda

/world/2026/oct/19/britain-geopolitical-.headline: No 10 leaves option open to impose Chinese EV tariffs if UK joins EU scheme
/world/2026/oct/19/britain-geopolitical-.excerpt: No 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”. Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme. The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme. The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures. The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”. “We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”. This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.
/world/2026/oct/19/britain-geopolitical-.trail: Beijing warns against ‘discriminatory’ step after France drops opposition to British role in Made in Europe package

/world/2026/oct/19/britain-geopolitical-.headline: Starlink access still not fully restored for Ukraine’s military, says Zelenskyy
/world/2026/oct/19/britain-geopolitical-.excerpt: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service has not yet been fully restored, as media reports suggested the order to throttle the service had come from within the White House. Zelenskyy met European leaders on Friday in Brussels, where he asked the EU for another €70bn (£60bn) next year to fund Ukraine’s defence against Russia. The meeting offered an important opportunity for Zelenskyy and Europe to align their strategies, as Zelenskyy once again found himself embroiled in a major quarrel with the US president, Donald Trump. Hours earlier, Trump had called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and criticised ⁠Zelenskyy, after a purported “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold. “All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher,” Trump told the Newsmax television channel. “Well, I think that’s a disgrace.” Energy analysts told the BBC that the US-Israeli war on Iran was having the biggest impact on diesel export volumes, although the Ukraine war was also significant. Trump’s administration is suspected of withholding intelligence from Ukraine on incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes, and of throttling Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite internet network, to prevent it from being used on drones flying faster than 100mph. Neither has officially been confirmed.
/world/2026/oct/19/britain-geopolitical-.trail: Ukrainian president says US limiting access was a ‘dangerous and unpleasant surprise’, amid reports the order came from inside White House

/politics/2026/oct/19/andy-burnham-launc.headline: Chiltern Railways enters public ownership in Labour nationalisation push
/politics/2026/oct/19/andy-burnham-launc.excerpt: Chiltern Railways has become the latest train operator to enter public ownership as the government closes in on its ambition to renationalise all major passenger rail services. The operator, which runs commuter rail services on the Chiltern mainline between London Marylebone and Birmingham, on Sunday became the sixth to be nationalised under Labour, with the remaining four to follow by the end of 2027. The Department for Transport (DfT) said the move would bring more reliable services, with plans to end what it termed the “daily frustration” of overcrowding. It has promised a package of improvements for Chiltern passengers, including more services and seats, new trains, upgraded stations and better onboard facilities including upgraded wifi. The government legislated in 2024 to renationalise private train operations as contracts allowed, joining the four operators already in public ownership and Network Rail to eventually establish an integrated body, Great British Railways (GBR). The rail minister, Peter Hendy, said: “Every transfer into public ownership gives us the chance to tackle the bread-and-butter issues people care about – more frequent, comfortable trains that turn up on time. “As we set up Great British Railways, we’re putting passengers first.
/politics/2026/oct/19/andy-burnham-launc.trail: Operator that runs services between London Marylebone and Birmingham is sixth to be nationalised since 2025

/politics/2026/oct/19/andy-burnham-launc.headline: Rail passengers get automatic right to switch operators for free when trains are cancelled
/politics/2026/oct/19/andy-burnham-launc.excerpt: Rail passengers whose trains are cancelled will have the immediate right to travel on other operators’ services to finish their journey without further charge, ministers have announced. The “commonsense change” will take effect from Sunday 20 September, ending the confusion in Britain where many pre-booked tickets are not valid on other firms’ trains. While passengers are frequently allowed to travel with different operators in times of severe disruption, travellers can be left to wait for a formal agreement that another firm’s tickets can be accepted, or sometimes buy an expensive new ticket and apply for a refund for the first. The Department for Transport said passengers had until now been “paying the price for a system which prioritises shareholders when trains are cancelled”. From 20 September, customers holding a valid ticket will be able to travel on another operator’s train two hours before or after the original cancelled service, on a reasonable alternative route. The rail minister, Lord Hendy, said: “This is a simple, commonsense change that puts passengers first. No one should be left stranded because of a fragmented railway when their journey is disrupted.
/politics/2026/oct/19/andy-burnham-launc.trail: ‘Commonsense change’ looks to end current confusion and put ‘passengers first, not shareholders’ when services are disrupted

/politics/2026/oct/19/andy-burnham-launc.headline: New battery-powered trains to ‘bring faster journeys to the north’
/politics/2026/oct/19/andy-burnham-launc.excerpt: A fleet of battery-powered trains is to be built to “bring faster, more reliable journeys to the north”, Downing Street has announced. The 29 trains, which will be run by TransPennine Express, will be built at Alstom’s Litchurch Lane works in Derby from 2028, supporting 350 local jobs, and nearly 6,000 across the UK, according to the government. The fleet will be made up of Adessia Stream trains, a battery-powered model that will be the first of its kind to be used for long-distance mainline journeys in the UK when it enters service in 2034. Andy Burnham, who has repeatedly championed public transport and now travels between No 10 offices in London and Manchester, highlighted the need for more reliable and efficient services, with the new trains pitched as making journeys between major northern cities shorter while increasing capacity on rail networks by 30% in the next decade. The trains will cut the journey time between Manchester and Leeds by up to 10 minutes, and between Manchester and York by up to 14 minutes. The prime minister said: “I’ve lost count of the number of times someone has stopped me to tell me about the train that never came. And when that happens, it means missed shifts, missed appointments and missed opportunities. “Today that starts to change. These 29 new trains will bring faster, more reliable journeys to the north, and thousands of British jobs for the next generation.
/politics/2026/oct/19/andy-burnham-launc.trail: No 10 says new fleet of trains built in Derby will support 6,000 jobs across UK

/politics/2026/oct/19/andy-burnham-launc.headline: Train operators to crack down on ‘donutters’ and other digital ticket cheats
/politics/2026/oct/19/andy-burnham-launc.excerpt: There is more than one way to commit fraud and, for some rail travellers, it has been as simple as a couple of taps on their phone as their train approaches its destination. That telltale last-minute purchase of a digital ticket – for the shortest journey that will allow them to bleep through the gates, regardless of how far they have travelled – is one of a number of illegal wheezes that train operators are trying to eliminate, with the enthusiastic backing of the government department that will directly oversee most of England’s rail services when they are renationalised next year. Two rail companies, South Western Railway (SWR) and GTR, which operates Thameslink, Southern and other services, this week introduced measures to clamp down on “short-faring” – a trick by which passengers buy a last-minute digital ticket only for the final part of their journey, even if they boarded in a station without barriers much further away. Don’t bother trying to download a digital ticket from Vauxhall to Waterloo, the terminus for many trains to London from the west – or on a number of other routes, apparently including from Norwood Junction to London Bridge, where many services from the south coast hit the capital. For those and some other routes, you will now need to collect a physical ticket from a physical ticket machine, after operators found that up to 95% of tickets on some short routes were being used fraudulently.
/politics/2026/oct/19/andy-burnham-launc.trail: South Western and GTR announce fightback after move away from paper tickets increases fare dodging

/politics/2026/oct/19/andy-burnham-launc.headline: A rail nightmare: what it’s like on England’s busiest commuter-only train
/politics/2026/oct/19/andy-burnham-launc.excerpt: The 5.46pm train from London Euston to Crewe is the low point of Nikhil Patel’s week. “I’ve never gotten a seat. I always stand up even when I get here early,” says the 22-year-old, struggling to keep his balance while the gangway underneath sways from side to side. Painfully for Patel, who is commuting back and forth to the capital for a computer science internship, it’s the first leg of a three-hour journey home to Walsall. He grabs the back of a chair to remain steady but says he’s just thankful that the train has left on time – and that it’s even on the move at all. “There’s been a couple of times where everyone’s boarded and then the train’s been cancelled and we all had to get off,” he says. On another occasion, his journey home took five hours because this service was delayed, meaning he missed a connecting train. This rush-hour service, operated by London Northwestern Railway (LNR), is the busiest commuter-only journey in England and Wales, according to figures by the Department for Transport. Overall, it’s the second busiest commute, the No 1 being a morning Thameslink service from Bedford to Three Bridges – which passes through three international hubs: St Pancras International, and Luton and Gatwick airports. We decided to join commuters getting the packed, two-hour-plus service on Thursday evening.
/politics/2026/oct/19/andy-burnham-launc.trail: This evening service from London to Crewe is hot, sweaty and heaving with people, many having to stand or sit in the gangways

/politics/2026/oct/18/police-investigate.headline: ‘Let’s see what he can do’: will Burnham bring voters back in Labour heartlands?
/politics/2026/oct/18/police-investigate.excerpt: Labour marked its worst performance in more than 50 years when voters went to the polls in Barnsley in May, but 100 days on from those seismic local elections, the political landscape has shifted drastically. Could the South Yorkshire town, where Reform UK reaped the benefits of dissatisfaction with Labour, prove to be a test case for whether the governing party has turned the tide? Labour had run Barnsley’s council since its inception in 1974, but was left with just 11 councillors after Reform triumphed with 42 seats. “I knew that it would be the most challenging set of elections that we’ve ever faced in Barnsley’s history,” said the councillor James Higginbottom, the new Labour group opposition leader. “What I didn’t necessarily expect was the scale of the Reform victory.” Catastrophic results in places such as Barnsley were a catalyst for Keir Starmer’s resignation. He has been replaced as prime minister by the former mayor of Greater Manchester Andy Burnham, who won the Labour leadership uncontested after a landslide byelection victory. Meanwhile, the Reform leader, Nigel Farage, is facing scrutiny over his financial affairs. While he was decisively re-elected in Clacton on Thursday, after he called a byelection in protest over a parliamentary standards investigation into his financial gifts, the contest was largely viewed as a sideshow after other major parties declined to stand. The parliamentary standards investigation has now resumed.
/politics/2026/oct/18/police-investigate.trail: With questions over Farage’s finances and a new face in No 10, could Barnsley council be a bellwether for changing Labour fortunes?

/environment/2026/oct/19/environment-cop.headline: Four years after the promises of Cop15, our biodiversity targets are slipping away
/environment/2026/oct/19/environment-cop.excerpt: The world has lost its way on nature once again. Next week, biodiversity Cop17 begins in Yerevan, Armenia, and expectations are low. Very low. Almost four years ago, governments reached an historic agreement at the biodiversity Cop15 to halt the destruction of Earth’s ecosystems – to rapturous applause in Montreal, Canada. I still remember the excitement in the hall in the early hours of that freezing December morning. Governments had never met a self-mandated target on biodiversity loss, but there was a sense after the Covid-19 pandemic that this time really would be different. The 23-point deal included targets to protect 30% of the planet for nature, restore 30% of the planet’s degraded terrestrial, inland water, coastal and marine ecosystems, and tackle $500bn of environmentally damaging subsidies. Almost every country in the world, apart from the US and the Vatican, backed it. Yes, the agreement was flawed, and barely matched what the science tells us we need to do to stop biodiversity loss. But it was a serious, considered plan to tackle the underlying causes of the largest loss of life since the dinosaurs (this time, humans are the asteroid). Since then, though, action has fallen short. More on why that is, what it means and what is at stake at Cop17, after this week’s climate headlines.
/environment/2026/oct/19/environment-cop.trail: ​The world pledged to halt biodiversity loss by 2030, but as Cop17 delegates meet in Armenia next week the outlook is bleak and optimism has faded

/world/2026/oct/18/killed-injured-russia.headline: Ukraine war briefing: Trump accuses Zelenskyy of not wanting to end war as feud rumbles on
/world/2026/oct/18/killed-injured-russia.excerpt: Donald Trump has defended his decision to waive some sanctions on Russia, while once again accusing Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war. “My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” the US president wrote on Truth Social. “Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” he added. Trump’s remarks come after he signed an executive order on Friday putting on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy. Earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy had thanked the Trump administration for resuming intelligence sharing between the two countries, but maintained the US had intentionally throttled its Starlink satellite internet access to send a “message” to Kyiv, write Andrew Roth and Sam Jones. Lithuania said Russia was likely behind an attempted arson attack on a company hosting communication hardware for Starlink satellites. Prime minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius made the claim on broadcaster LRT after authorities discovered flammable liquids at the company in question. Sinkevicius said the firm, whose location he did not mention, houses “nine satellite antennas to guarantee the Starlink connection, which of course supports and assists Ukraine”.

/world/2026/oct/18/killed-injured-russia.headline: Intensifying drone attacks on ships in Black Sea bring war ever closer to Nato shores
/world/2026/oct/18/killed-injured-russia.excerpt: The first the crew of the Bulgarian ferry Dioscuria knew of an attack on a cargo ship in their country’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea in the early hours of 6 October was a distant explosion 70 miles off the coastal town of Byala. The Turkish-owned Alfa Watan, heading for the Romanian port of Sulina, had been struck by suspected Russian air and naval drones. Arriving on the scene, Dioscuria found an overturned lifeboat and lifejackets in the water. There was no sign, however, of Alfa Watan’s crew of 10. Six days later drones struck another ship off the coast of Bulgaria, HS Dignity. Eleven crew members died. By Thursday, the attacks had encroached on Romania’s airspace and territorial water. Two chemical tankers, Wine Trader and Yara J, were attacked and left burning. Seven more sailors were missing. The attacks on six ships in 10 days – the Able and Chelsea-3 were also hit – marked a dramatic escalation in a maritime conflict that is pressing on Nato’s borders. While global attention has focused on the risks for sailors travelling through the strait of Hormuz, in recent months it is the Black Sea that has emerged as the more dangerous passage, with more sailors lost in a week and a half than US service members killed in the entire Iran war. The maritime insurer and risk analyst Ambrey has warned that there is no end in sight to the threats to Black Sea cargo shipping, including grain and oil, and that insurance prices for passage of the waters have rocketed.

The Ukrainian president also said he expected the Trump administration to lift more sanctions against Russia in the future and called for Europe to establish its own negotiations with Moscow as the US has sought better ties and business deals with the Kremlin. “Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue, and I believe that the ‘diesel deal’ is the first step,” said Zelenskyy on Saturday. “Unfortunately, it seems to me that this cannot stop Putin; on the contrary, he feels joy and happiness that he has such support.” In a social media message, Zelenskyy wrote: “A US ⁠sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking. We must not give up ground. “We must keep trying to end the ‌war. To end it, not give Putin every reason to continue it indefinitely.” In the Trump administration’s latest effort to reduce tensions with Russia, the US president announced on Friday that he would put a hold on a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause on the legislation passed by both chambers was in the national interest.

The president of the German Bundesbank, Joachim Nagel, said nearly half of all delegates took part in the joint departure when Siluanov started speaking. “The Ukraine war is existential for us in Europe,” one European diplomat told the Reuters news agency. “We cannot normalise relations with Russia.” The walkout was acknowledged by the chair of the IMF’s steering committee, the Saudi finance minister, Mohammed al-Jadaan.
